nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: When are cover crops typically grown?
nodes.answer: Cover crops are mostly grown during autumn and winter, in the time between main crops.

The upgrading to transport fuel offers an envi- ronmentally favorable alternative compared to com- bustion in CHP units (Styles et al. 2016). Nutrients in the organic input material are mostly retained in the residue after digestion, the digestate, which can be used as a bio-based fertilizer to recycle nutrients back to agricultural fields. The recent expansion of biogas production across Europe (Gustafsson & Anderberg 2022) has resulted in a lack of energy-rich feedstocks such as slaughterhouse waste. Potential supple- mentary feedstocks for biogas production which are receiving growing interest are cover crops (Feng et al. 2020). Cover crops are grown to reduce leaching of nutri- ents and soil erosion when there is no main crop in the field, i.e. in the time between main crops, mostly dur - ing autumn and winter.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Conservation farming|Cover cropping methods_qna_002
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: Why are cover crops important in organic farming systems?
nodes.answer: Cover crops, including legumes, contribute significantly to the nitrogen input for main crops in organic farming systems.
nodes.paragraph: Various species can be used, and mixtures of species can provide a variety of ser - vices (Justes 2017). Legumes can be used to increase the nitrogen (N) input to the soil through biological N fixation from the atmosphere (Tribouillois et al. 2016; Herridge et al. 2008). Cover crops, including legumes, are important especially in organic farm- ing systems, where they contribute with a significant share of the input of N to the main crops (Berry et al. 2006). In organic farming, synthetic chemicals are not allowed, including fertilizers, herbicides and pes- ticides (EC 2023; Hansen et al. 2001). Protection of ecological, human, and animal health are key motiva- tors for the expansion of organic farming in Denmark, which is the country with the highest market share of organic food in the world (EU CAP Network 2023). In organic farming, nutrient sources include agricul- tural waste and animal manure produced on the farm, and biological N fixation (Watson et al. 2006).

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: How can the problem of high moisture content in cover crops be addressed?
nodes.answer: The problem can be combated by co-ensiling cover crops with straw.
nodes.paragraph: 2017). A poten- tial problem with the ensiling of cover crops is their relatively high moisture content at the time of har - vest, which may cause problems for the fermentation. Such problems may be combated by co-ensiling cover crops with straw (Feng et al. 2019). To avoid losses of straw before the harvesting of cover crops and limit the number of field operations, the most viable strat- egy is to harvest the straw at the time of harvest of the main crop and store it until the cover crops also have been harvested (Fontaine et al. 2020a). Cover crops and other agricultural residues are not commonly used as exclusive feedstock in biogas plants (Feng et al. 2020; Thamsiriroj et al. 2012; Xie 215 Nutr Cycl Agroecosyst (2025) 130:213 232 Vol. : (123456789) et al. 2011). Common practice is to co-digest with animal manure (Feng et al. 2020). The implementa- tion of technology for anaerobic digestion of cover crops is thus most feasible at animal farms, where co- digestion with animal manure is possible.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Conservation farming|Cover cropping methods_qna_005
nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: How are cover crops typically utilized in relation to the main crop?
nodes.answer: Cover crops are sown either around the same time as the main crop (under-sowing) or immediately after the harvest of the main crop.
nodes.paragraph: Leg- umes thus have an important role in organic farming, enabling higher crop yields than would otherwise be feasible without synthetic N fertilizer. Cover crops are sown either around the same time as the main crop (under-sowing) or immedi- lately after harvest of the main crop. Under-sowing allows a longer growing period of the cover crops and can improve their establishment (De Notaris et al. 2019; Liu et al. 2015). Generally, cover crops are not harvested, but the biomass is left in the field to decompose, so that nutrients are released and can be available for the succeeding crop (Askegaard & Erik - sen 2007; Tribouillois et al. 2016). However, if suffi- cient biomass can be attained, an attractive alternative could be to harvest the cover crop biomass and use this as feedstock in anaerobic digestion. Potentially this could result in benefits both in terms of increased biogas production and improved nutrient manage- ment in the field. The main point of anaerobic digestion is to pro- duce biogas, but another effect is that part of the organic N compounds are mineralized into ammo- nium N, which is readily available for plant uptake.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Conservation farming|Cover cropping methods_qna_007
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What are the environmental benefits of harvesting cover crops mentioned in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: Harvesting cover crops can lead to avoided emissions of ammonia and nitrous oxide during their decomposition in the field and prevent nitrate leaching that occurs during periods of low crop demand.
nodes.paragraph: Fertilization with digestate could thus increase the share of directly plant-available N, which can be field applied at the right time to meet crop demand (Fon- taine et al. 2020a, b; M ller & M ller 2012). This could increase the N uptake efficiency, contributing to improved yields and lower losses of N to the envi- ronment (DCE 2021; Fr seth et al. 2014). Harvesting of cover crops could also lead to avoided emissions from their decomposition in the field, such as ammo- nia and nitrous oxide (Fr seth et al. 2014; Nadeem et al. 2012), and leaching of nitrate, which can take place when nitrate is released at times of low crop demand (DCE 2021). The harvesting and later appli- cation of digestate could thus result in more efficient nutrient use by the crops and lower emissions to the environment. To enable continuous operation of a biogas plant, a storage solution is needed to preserve the cover crop biomass until it can be fed to the biogas reac- tor.
